title: Mark Fisher
summary: Mark Fisher was a British philosopher, music critic and teacher who wrote about how the economy and culture seep into the way we feel. His “capitalist realism” is the widespread sense that the existing order is the only one possible and that an alternative to it can’t even be imagined. Fisher combined analysis of pop music, film and everyday life with one question: why do so many people feel exhausted and depressed?
onEmotions: Fisher’s central idea about feelings is that they can’t be fully understood if we look only inside a single person. He called this “the privatization of stress”: society teaches us to regard anxiety, depression and fatigue as purely personal problems, although they also have social causes — precarious work, competition, debt, a sense that the future has been closed off. This view doesn’t cancel your personal history, but it lifts some of the guilt. Fisher also wrote about “hauntology” — the feeling of being haunted by the ghosts of futures that never arrived — and about how collectively recognizing shared difficulties can itself bring relief.

anxiety.text: The anxiety you feel is understandable and deserves compassion, not reproach. Fisher would look at where it comes from. He wrote about “the privatization of stress”: we are taught to see anxiety as a strictly personal malfunction — faulty brain chemistry or a weak character — even though many of its sources lie outside us. Unstable work, constant evaluation, the need to keep “selling yourself,” an unclear tomorrow — all this creates a background against which anxiety is natural. Fisher didn’t deny the personal dimension, but he insisted: if millions are anxious, it isn’t only about each of them. Knowing this can lighten the load. Your anxiety is not only your fault; it is also a response to real conditions that many people share with you.
anxiety.practice: Make two columns: “what in my anxiety is connected to my own history” and “what is connected to circumstances many people share.” Just look at them.

quote.text: The current ruling ontology denies any possibility of a social causation of mental illness.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

fear.text: Fear is a natural reaction to uncertainty, and you have every right to feel it. Fisher described a world in which uncertainty has become the norm: a job can end at any moment, the future isn’t guaranteed, and responsibility for everything is placed on the individual. He noted that the flexibility and instability presented as freedom turn, for many people, into chronic fear. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that fear is not only a personal trait but a reasonable response to conditions in which a person has little to lean on. This understanding helps you stop blaming yourself for being afraid. And it suggests where to look for support: not only in your own resilience, but in other people who fear the same things.
fear.practice: Think about whom you could talk to about what frightens you — not to solve it, just so you don’t have to hold it alone.

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and it doesn’t need to be hidden behind a cheerful smile. Fisher was one of the first to write openly about depression as a political question, not only a private one. He noticed that in a culture demanding constant positivity and “motivation,” sadness looks like personal failure. But in his view, sorrow often responds to a real loss — the loss of community, of stability, of faith in a better future. Fisher wrote about “the slow cancellation of the future”: the feeling that the new things progress promised never actually arrived. From this point of view, your sadness may not be a malfunction but a sensitivity to what is genuinely missing. It can be shared with others — and in the sharing it grows lighter.
sadness.practice: Ask yourself: am I sad only about my own life — or also about something that many people around me are missing?

grief.text: Grief is a deep and natural experience of loss, and it needs no deadlines and no justification. Fisher wrote a great deal about ghosts — not mystical ones but cultural ones: about how the past goes on sounding in the present. He called this “hauntology,” from the word “haunt.” In Ghosts of My Life he describes music that sounds like a memory, like traces of what has gone but won’t let go. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that the continued presence of what you’ve lost in your life is not a refusal to accept it but a form of faithfulness. Ghosts, as he saw them, don’t just frighten — they preserve what was valuable. Your grief can live beside you as memory, not as a wound that must be closed at once.
grief.practice: Find a song, a scent or an object in which what you’ve lost lives on for you, and spend a few minutes with it.

loneliness.text: Loneliness is painful, and feeling it doesn’t make you weak or strange. Fisher would point out that loneliness is not only a personal experience but a feature of the age. He wrote that modern society breaks up older forms of community — trade unions, neighborly ties, shared places — and turns everyone into a separate competitor. At the same time, difficulties are privatized too: everyone thinks they suffer alone. Fisher recalled the practice of “consciousness-raising” — meetings at which people discovered that their “personal” problems were shared. From this point of view, your loneliness is partly a consequence of how the world is arranged, not evidence that you are unfit for connection. And it can ease simply from discovering that others feel the same.
loneliness.practice: Think about which of the people you know might be feeling a similar loneliness right now. Could you send them a short message?

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate response to injustice or powerlessness, and there’s no need to be ashamed of it. Fisher noticed something interesting: in today’s world anger often finds no outside target and turns inward. People get angry with themselves for not coping, instead of seeing the circumstances that make “coping” almost impossible. Fisher called one consequence of this “reflexive impotence”: people understand that things are bad but are convinced nothing can be changed — and this conviction becomes self-fulfilling. From this point of view, your anger is not a destructive force but a sign that you haven’t resigned yourself yet. It can be directed not against yourself but toward understanding what is really wrong.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: who or what is my anger aimed at — myself, or my circumstances? What would change if I redirected it?

shame.text: Shame is one of the heaviest feelings, and you deserve to treat yourself gently in it. Fisher wrote openly about shame tied to class and background — the feeling of being “out of place,” of having nothing to say in spaces where others feel confident. In his essay “Good For Nothing” he described how society convinces people that their position is entirely deserved, so that their difficulties become a cause for shame. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that part of your shame is society’s internalized judgment, not the truth about you. Seeing this is already a liberation. Shame loses its power when we understand that its source lies not only inside us but in how the hierarchy around us is built.
shame.practice: Write down a sentence your inner voice uses to shame you, and ask: where did I first hear it — and whose thought is it really?

guilt.text: Guilt shows that you care, and that in itself is valuable. But Fisher would help you distinguish guilt over a specific act from a vague, constant feeling that you are “not trying hard enough.” The latter, in his view, is largely created by a culture that loads the individual with responsibility for everything: career, health, well-being, even economic crises. Fisher called this privatization: shared problems are turned into personal failures. From this point of view, you could say: if you’re to blame for everything, something is wrong with the frame itself. Separating real responsibility from imposed guilt can bring relief: the first can be put right, the second can be let go as a burden that isn’t yours.
guilt.practice: Divide your guilt into two parts: “a specific act I can put right” and “a feeling that I’m not enough in general.” Which part are you actually dealing with right now?

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but very understandable feeling, and admitting it is already a step toward being honest with yourself. Fisher would explain why there is so much of it today. The world he described as “capitalist realism” turns life into an endless competition: for jobs, for attention, for a place in the rankings. When success is considered entirely a personal achievement, every success of someone else’s inevitably sounds like a reproach to you. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that envy is not a trait of your character but a natural side effect of a system built on competition. This understanding lets you soften both toward yourself and toward the person you envy: you are both taking part in the same race, which neither of you chose, and perhaps you are both tired of it.
envy.practice: Ask yourself: if there were no comparison and no rankings at all, would I want the same thing this person has?

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are exhausting, and the fact that they are hard to explain doesn’t make them any less real. Fisher wrote a great deal about this state — including from his own experience. He noticed in his students, and in himself, what he called “depressive hedonia”: a person is not so much unable to get pleasure as unable to do anything except pursue it — scroll, switch, consume. And yet there is no deep satisfaction. Fisher linked this to a culture of endless stimulation and to the feeling that the future is closed and there is nothing to strive for. This view can bring relief: your emptiness is not a personal defect but a response to a world in which it is hard to find a large, shared, meaningful cause. And it doesn’t tell the whole truth about you.
emptiness.practice: Recall at least one activity after which you felt not “that was pleasant” but “that was meaningful.” What was different about it?

confusion.text: Confusion is a normal reaction to a world that’s hard to understand, and you don’t need to pretend everything is clear. Fisher wrote that one feature of our time is the sense that the existing order of things is the only one possible. He called this “capitalist realism”: an atmosphere in which it is hard even to imagine anything else. Confusion can arise precisely where old explanations stop working and new ones haven’t yet appeared. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say this is not a weakness of mind but a moment when the familiar picture of the world cracks. He believed such cracks are valuable — through them you can see that the “natural order” was in fact made by people and could be different. Confusion is the beginning of a new question.
confusion.practice: Write down one belief you’ve started to doubt, and add: “What if it could be otherwise?”

fatigue.text: Your fatigue is real, and it doesn’t mean you are lazy or weak. Fisher described burnout as one of the mass conditions of our time. He pointed to bureaucracy which, contrary to promises, hasn’t disappeared but has only grown: endless reports, metrics, self-assessments, the need to constantly prove your efficiency. Add to that instability and the feeling that you can’t stop. Fisher insisted that if so many people are exhausted at once, it can’t be explained only by the personal shortcomings of each. This understanding lifts some of the guilt: your fatigue is a response to a real overload. You don’t have to “overcome” it. You can give it room, acknowledge that it’s legitimate, and share it with others who are just as tired.
fatigue.practice: Notice what part of your fatigue comes not from the work itself but from reports, evaluations and proving your usefulness.

boredom.text: Boredom can be agonizing, and there is nothing shameful in it. Fisher described a distinctly modern boredom — not the kind that comes from having nothing to do, but the kind born amid an endless abundance of entertainment. We are constantly plugged into a stream of content, yet nothing truly absorbs us. He wrote about students who couldn’t tear themselves away from their screens but didn’t get any joy from them either. From Fisher’s perspective, this kind of boredom is not a whim but a sign that the stream of stimuli lacks anything genuinely new. He regretted that culture increasingly repeats the past instead of inventing the future. Your boredom may be a healthy feeling — a longing for something truly new that hasn’t yet been invented.
boredom.practice: Ask yourself: what genuinely new thing am I missing — not another distraction, but something that would change how I see?

quote.text: …the condition I’m referring to is constituted not by an inability to get pleasure so much as by an inability to do anything else except pursue pleasure.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

joy.text: Joy is a precious feeling, and you have every right to give yourself to it fully. Fisher, often known as the author of gloomy books, actually thought a great deal about joy. Especially collective joy: the dance floor, the concert, the shared movement in which people experience something greater than personal pleasure. In his last years he was working on an idea he called “acid communism” — about how to restore to society the capacity for a shared dream and the joy of freeing consciousness. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that joy is not just a pleasant sensation but a reminder that life could be different from the familiar routine. It is especially worth cherishing and sharing — shared joy holds the promise of a different future.
joy.practice: Think about whom you could share this joy with — call them, tell them, invite them somewhere together.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the most valuable experiences, and you don’t need to be shy about them. Fisher didn’t write a separate theory of love, but from the standpoint of his ideas something important can be said. He showed how market logic seeps into the most varied spheres of life, turning people into competitors and relationships into deals. Against this background, love and tenderness turn out to be forms of resistance: they don’t submit to calculations of profit, and they bind people together beyond usefulness. Fisher valued solidarity and care as what stands against loneliness and the privatization of suffering. Your tenderness is not a weakness in a harsh world but evidence that human bonds are stronger than the logic of competition. It is worth protecting.
love.practice: Recall a recent moment of tenderness — your own or someone else’s. What was there in it that can’t be measured or exchanged?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling that connects you with other people. Fisher didn’t write about it specifically, but from the standpoint of his thought you could say that gratitude dismantles the illusion of complete self-sufficiency. The society he criticized insists that everyone is the sole author of their own fate, and everything achieved is purely personal merit. Gratitude shows the opposite: we live thanks to others — those who taught us, cared for us, made the music and books that sustained us. Fisher himself wrote a lot about how culture and community saved him in hard times. Gratitude brings you back to the understanding that you are part of a web of mutual support, not a lonely entrepreneur of yourself.
gratitude.practice: Name one person or one work — a song, a book, a film — that helped you through a hard time, and silently thank them.

hope.text: Hope is an important feeling, especially when everything seems frozen. Fisher knew how hard it is to hope: his major book describes an atmosphere in which it is impossible to imagine anything else. But it doesn’t end in despair. Fisher wrote that the very sense that nothing can change makes any change unexpected and powerful. Capitalist realism, in his view, is strong only as long as people believe in it; a small crack is enough for the horizon to open again. From this point of view, your hope is not naivety but a sober understanding that a world made by people can change. It doesn’t have to be big — it only needs to be enough to keep you from accepting the current state of things as final.
hope.practice: Remember something in your life or in the world that once seemed impossible but happened. How does that change your hope now?

quote.text: The tiniest event can tear a hole in the grey curtain of reaction which has marked the horizons of possibility under capitalist realism.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm, aching feeling, and you don’t need to defend yourself against it. Fisher thought about it very carefully. He distinguished two kinds: nostalgia that simply longs for old things, and what he called “hauntology” — a longing not so much for the past as for the futures that past promised but that never arrived. In Ghosts of My Life he hears in the music of his youth the promise of a world that might have been. From this point of view, your nostalgia may speak not only of what you have lost but also of what you hoped for. This is valuable knowledge: the ghosts of the past keep dreams that can still be brought back into the present.
nostalgia.practice: Think about what you miss, and ask yourself: what promise about the future was hidden in that time?

craving.text: A sharp “I want it right now” can be very strong, and it doesn’t make you a weak person. Fisher described a state he called “depressive hedonia”: we are not so much unable to get pleasure as unable to do anything except pursue it — one more video, one more cigarette, one more drink, one more refresh of the feed. He saw this not as a personal vice but as a symptom of a culture that offers endless quick stimuli instead of meaning and a shared cause. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that a craving often promises to switch off the background hum of pressure and emptiness for a minute. That doesn’t cancel its force, but it changes the question — not “what’s wrong with me?” but “what am I really missing?” The wave of wanting rises and falls; it can be waited out.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, ask yourself: “If this weren’t a thing but a need — for rest, connection, meaning — which would it be?” Write down the answer and watch how the wave changes.

addiction.text: If your life has long revolved around something that’s hard to get out of, that is hard, and it is not a moral failure. Fisher insisted that our suffering can’t be understood only as a “personal problem.” He criticized “the privatization of stress” — the habit of explaining everything by brain chemistry or willpower while ignoring loneliness, precarious work, a closed-off future. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that addiction often grows where the shared world collapses — community, support, the sense that life could be different. This doesn’t take away the weight of the circle, but it does remove some of the shame. Fisher believed in the power of the collective: that people who recognize shared difficulties together change more easily than they do alone. Getting out of the circle isn’t only a personal feat either; others can take part in it.
addiction.practice: Consider whether there is a person or a community nearby who understands this path from the inside — for example, a mutual-help group. Just write down who it might be, with no obligation to do anything today.

hangover.text: A hangover — in body and soul, with anxiety, shame and gaps in memory — is a very unpleasant state, and you deserve gentleness. Fisher would suggest taking a closer look at the “moral hangover.” Morning shame usually sounds like a verdict on your whole person: “I’ve ruined everything again.” But Fisher wrote a lot about how society privatizes feelings: everything that happens to us is declared to be solely our fault and our responsibility. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that behind last night there is often an understandable wish — to breathe out, to feel part of something shared, to step out for a while from the mode of endless functioning. That wish is legitimate, even if the way it was met has left a heavy mark. Today you don’t need to pass sentence on yourself. You can simply take care of yourself and ask what the real need was.
hangover.practice: Put self-criticism off until tomorrow. Today, answer only one question: “What did I really need last night — rest, people, freedom?”

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid experience in which everything seems possible. You can enjoy it. Fisher valued exactly this feeling — the sense that the world could be different. He wrote that “capitalist realism” trains us to think there are no alternatives and the future is already closed. Moments of elation when that feeling suddenly lifts he considered precious — especially shared ones: at a concert, in dance, in a conversation where a new idea is born. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that euphoria is a glimpse of an open future. So that it doesn’t fade without a trace, it helps not only to live it but to remember it: what exactly seemed possible? Whom would you like to share it with? A question like that turns a flash into something you can come back to later.
euphoria.practice: Write down one sentence: “In that moment, it seemed possible to…” — and keep it to reread on an ordinary day.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high can be very painful: the world suddenly turns grey again. It’s an understandable reaction, not your fault. Fisher often described a similar state at the level of a whole culture. Following Franco “Bifo” Berardi, he spoke of “the slow cancellation of the future”: the feeling that the bright tomorrow we were promised never arrived and life has fallen back into the usual rut. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say the comedown is hard partly because the high was a glimpse of another possibility, and the drop seems to prove there isn’t one. But Fisher insisted: greyness is not the nature of things but a condition that changes. What you saw during the high was not an illusion but a hint. For now, you can simply wait it out and take care of yourself.
crash.practice: Write: “The drop is not proof that the good things weren’t real.” Add one thing that could give you at least a little support today.

panic.text: Panic is terrifying: your heart pounds, you can’t get enough air, it seems something irreversible is about to happen. It’s a very hard experience, and you are not alone in it. Fisher would point out that millions of people go through such states today, and he saw in this not only a personal but a social dimension: constant uncertainty, instability, living “braced for the next blow.” He said that stress has been privatized — everyone carries it alone, as if it were their own private malfunction. Right now, in the middle of the wave, explanations aren’t the main thing. The main thing is that a wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don’t have to fight it; you can wait it out, leaning on your body, on the floor beneath your feet, on what is around you.
panic.practice: Put your feet flat on the floor, make your exhale longer than your inhale, and slowly name five objects you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — the question “what is all this for,” the sense of an abyss — is one of the deepest human experiences, and it doesn’t make you weak. In The Weird and the Eerie, Fisher wrote about feelings that arise at the edge of the familiar world: the “weird” — the presence of something that doesn’t belong here — and the “eerie” — the sense that something unfathomable lies behind what we see. These experiences are unsettling, but Fisher also saw value in them: they let us look at the familiar from outside and understand that the world is bigger than our routines. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your dread is also an encounter with a vastness that everyday life usually screens off. In it you can not only get lost but also find questions that give life back its depth.
dread.practice: Write down one question rising out of this dread right now — without answering it. Then place a hand on your chest and take a few slow exhales.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are in the wrong place is familiar to many, and there is nothing shameful in it. Fisher wrote a lot about digital culture, in which we are always “connected” and always see other people’s lives in their best shots. He noted that such an environment turns everyone into an entrepreneur of their own life, forced to constantly compare and sell themselves. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that the fear of missing out is neither personal envy nor foolishness, but a response to the design of an environment that deliberately keeps a sense of lack alive. A great many people share this feeling with you — including those whose pictures make you envious. Realizing this is already a relief: you are not the only one “in the wrong place.”
fomo.practice: Choose one feed or app and remove it from your home screen for a day. Notice how the feeling of “I’m missing something” changes.

sleepless.text: A sleepless night, three-in-the-morning thoughts going round in circles — it’s exhausting, and it’s not your fault. Fisher wrote about precarious, “flexible” work that doesn’t end when the working day does: messages, deadlines and anxiety about the future seep into every hour of the day. Jonathan Crary developed a related idea in his book 24/7, where sleep is described as the last thing that resists the demand to be always available. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that night-time anxiety is also an echo of life without clear boundaries, not only your personal inability to “switch off.” At three in the morning everything looks darker than it is. The thoughts that come at that hour don’t have to be solved now.
sleepless.practice: Write your worrying thoughts down on paper and add: “This is a question for daylight.” Turn the sheet over and return to your breathing.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only your bond with a person but the feeling that you can lean on others. It is real pain. Fisher didn’t write specifically about betrayal in personal relationships, but from the standpoint of his thought something important can be said. He showed how contemporary culture trains us to see others as competitors and to treat relationships as deals. In such an environment trust becomes especially fragile — and especially precious. Yet Fisher never gave up his belief in solidarity: he thought people are capable of genuine mutuality if the conditions for it are created. One person’s betrayal doesn’t cancel that possibility. Your capacity to trust is not naivety but what everything good between people rests on.
betrayal.practice: Recall one person who once didn’t let you down. Write them a few words, or simply thank them in your mind.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is an agonizing and very human feeling, and there’s no need to shame yourself for it. Fisher didn’t write about jealousy specifically, but from the standpoint of his ideas you could say this: we live in a culture that teaches us to see the world as a market, where everything is compared, rated and replaceable. Even love starts, without our meaning it to, to look like competition — with others, with imagined “better options.” Hence the fear that you might be “traded in.” This doesn’t mean your jealousy is imagined: there is a great deal of real attachment and vulnerability in it. But it helps to notice which part of the fear belongs not only to you but to a general background of comparison and insecurity. Relationships, as Fisher saw it, can be a place where this market logic doesn’t apply.
jealousy.practice: Write: “What am I really afraid of — losing the person, or turning out to be ‘not good enough’?” Note which part of that is about your relationship and which is about the general background of comparison.

resentment.text: An old grievance is a weight you carry around. Often it keeps the memory of a real injustice, and that deserves to be acknowledged. Fisher would suggest looking at the grievance more broadly. He wrote about “consciousness-raising” — a practice in which people share their experiences and discover that their private pain is connected to shared conditions. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that a grievance becomes especially heavy when we carry it alone and see in it only a personal story between two people. When you manage to see the wider context too — the power, inequality and pressure that everyone involved was under — the grievance doesn’t vanish, but it can stop eating away at you from the inside. Your sense of justice is valuable; it can be directed not only at the past but at what can still be changed.
resentment.practice: Write down what happened to you, and then one line: “What circumstances — not only the person — made this possible?”

heartbreak.text: A broken heart really hurts, and there’s no need to hurry that pain along. Fisher wrote a great deal about “hauntology” — about how we are haunted by ghosts: a past that won’t let go, and unrealized futures that keep sounding. He especially loved music in which this ghostliness can be heard — for example, Burial’s records, with their muffled voices like echoes of nights gone by and people lost. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that after a breakup the person becomes such a ghost for us, and with them the future you had imagined together. Grieving it is natural. Fisher showed that ghosts don’t only wound: they preserve what was valuable. In time they can become not pain but memory.
heartbreak.practice: Put on music that exactly matches your feeling, and let yourself be sad to it for a few minutes, without trying to “cheer up.”

impostor.text: The fear that you’re about to be found out is familiar to a great many people, and it says nothing about your real worth. Fisher would help you see its social roots. In his essay “Good For Nothing,” he wrote about how class background and social position shape the feeling that you have no right to be where you are — at university, in a profession, in a conversation. This feeling is instilled over years, and then it sounds like your own voice. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that impostor syndrome is often not the truth about you but the trace of social hierarchies that decide in advance who “belongs” and who is an “outsider.” Once you recognize this mechanism, you can step back from your fear a little: it’s loud, but it isn’t a judge.
impostor.practice: Write: “Who once made me understand that I didn’t belong here?” Then: “What did I actually do to get here?”

self_hatred.text: If your inner voice is cruel to you, that is very hard, and you deserve compassion — including from yourself. What this voice says is not the truth about you. Fisher wrote openly about dark states and about the voice that insists you are good for nothing. He came to the view that this voice is largely absorbed from outside: society teaches us to blame ourselves for things tied to inequality, instability and constant evaluation. In his essay “Good For Nothing,” he showed how a sense of one’s own worthlessness can be a reflection of social position rather than a person’s essence. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your inner critic speaks in a voice you didn’t invent. You don’t have to believe it.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic. Next to it write: “Whose voice is this really? Where did I pick it up?”

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling, especially when it seems nothing can be changed. It is understandable and deserves compassion. Fisher described a similar state in his students and called it “reflexive impotence.” People understand that much is badly arranged, and “know” just as clearly that they can do nothing about it. But Fisher noticed something important: this knowledge is not a neutral observation but partly a self-fulfilling prophecy. The certainty of being powerless itself keeps us from acting. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your powerlessness is real, but it isn’t the whole truth. Much really is beyond your control — and that isn’t your fault. But sometimes a single small action is enough for the prophecy to stop coming true.
helplessness.practice: Name one very small thing you can do today — write to someone, tidy one corner, make one call. Do only that.

quote.text: They know things are bad, but more than that, they know they can’t do anything about it. But that “knowledge”, that reflexivity, is not a passive observation of an already existing state of affairs. It is a self-fulfilling prophecy.
quote.author: Mark Fisher

procrastination.text: “I can’t get started” is not laziness or a character flaw. Fisher would help lift some of the shame. He wrote about how work and study are saturated with endless reports, metrics and audits — he called this “market Stalinism”: the system cares more about how a result looks than about the work itself. When a task seems like a pointless formality, starting it is especially hard. Fisher also described “depressive hedonia” — the constant pull of quick stimuli that makes concentration agonizing. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your procrastination may signal not weakness but a loss of meaning, or overload. You can ask yourself not “why am I like this?” but “what about this task drains its meaning for me?”
procrastination.practice: Write one line: “Why does this task matter to me personally — not for the report, but for me?” Then do the first two minutes of work.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — emigration, a move, losing your ground — changes life profoundly, and your sense of loss is legitimate. Fisher wrote a great deal about place and memory. In Ghosts of My Life he described how we are haunted by ghosts — of a past that won’t let go, and of futures that never arrived. The place you left keeps sounding in you like such a ghost: streets, smells, language, people. Fisher also showed how the modern world demands “flexibility” and mobility, forcing people to keep moving and adapting. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your uprootedness is not only a personal failure to adapt but a shared experience of the age. The ghosts of home are not enemies; they keep what was dear to you.
uprooted.practice: Write down three details from the place you left: a sound, a smell, a view. Consider whether you could bring one of them back into your life now.

overload.text: Overload from the stream of news, messages and the endless feed is real exhaustion, not your inability to “cope.” Fisher, following Franco “Bifo” Berardi, wrote about the overloading of the “infosphere”: the volume of signals demanding attention has long exceeded what a person can process. He noticed in his students a state of constant connection — phone, headphones, feed — with not a minute of silence or concentration. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your exhaustion is the nervous system’s natural response to an environment deliberately designed to hold attention. This is not a personal weakness. The way out isn’t learning to consume even more, even faster, but stepping out of the stream from time to time — and knowing you’re not alone in this.
overload.practice: Turn off notifications for an hour. Notice how your breathing and attention change when nothing demands an immediate reply.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real can be strange and unsettling. It deserves gentle care. Fisher thought a lot about what we call “reality.” His “capitalist realism” is the idea that the familiar order of things seems to us the only possible and natural one, even though it was largely made by people and could be different. In The Weird and the Eerie, he described experiences in which the familiar world suddenly looks alien. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that a sense of unreality sometimes arises when the familiar picture of the world loses its persuasiveness. It’s frightening, but it doesn’t make you “abnormal.” You can gently lean on what is tangible here and now: your body, sounds, objects, people.
unreality.practice: Name aloud three things you can hear and three you can touch. Rest your hand on one of them.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and valuable experience, worth savoring fully. In The Weird and the Eerie, Fisher wrote about the feelings that arise when we meet what lies beyond the familiar. He noted that such experiences don’t only unsettle but also fascinate: they let us see the familiar world from outside and feel that it is bigger than our routines. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that awe is the moment when the “realism” of everyday life, with its reports and tasks, suddenly stops being the only reality. Something vast opens up — the sea, the sky, music, another person’s thought. Fisher valued such moments as a reminder that the world is neither exhausted nor closed.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with whatever filled you with awe. Then write down one word that describes how the world seemed to you in that moment.

relief.text: Relief is a warm, well-earned feeling: something heavy has finally let go. You can simply enjoy it. Fisher wrote a lot about the relief that comes when a person realizes their difficulties are shared by others. He called this “consciousness-raising”: when people tell each other about their experiences, private, shameful pain turns into something shared, understandable and explicable. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that relief is the moment when the burden stops being yours alone. Even if you experience it in solitude, there is something of that discovery in it: life is bigger than you thought at the hardest moment. You can remember this moment — and share it with someone.
relief.practice: If you like, tell someone that you feel better — in a single sentence, in a message or out loud.

calm.text: Calm and peace are a precious state, and you can simply be in it. Fisher didn’t write about calm specifically, but from the standpoint of his thought you could say that in a culture of constant connection, where everything demands attention and reaction, calm is rare, almost a luxury. Fisher criticized an environment with not a minute of silence, and dreamed of a life in which people have time not only to work and consume but simply to be, to think, to listen. Your calm is a small piece of such a life. It doesn’t need to be used for anything or justified. You can simply notice it and let it last — as a reminder that another rhythm of life is possible already, right now.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute without touching your phone, and notice what you hear around you — the near sounds and the far ones.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a lively, joyful feeling, and it’s worth meeting with gratitude. Fisher would have been glad of it: he believed our culture suffers from a shortage of the new. He wrote about “the slow cancellation of the future” — the sense that instead of new forms we endlessly recycle old ones. He saw the opposite of this in “popular modernism”: times when bold, experimental ideas reached huge numbers of people through music, books and television. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your inspiration is a small breakthrough of the future into the present, a glimpse of what hasn’t existed yet. It’s worth protecting, without rushing to fit it to familiar measures of success. Sometimes the most valuable thing about a new idea is that it doesn’t yet resemble anything.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea that came to you, and one sentence about what is genuinely new in it — something you haven’t seen before.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is a shameful pleasure known to a great many people. Fisher wrote about “business ontology” — the conviction that everything in society, from hospitals to schools, should be run like a business. In such an environment life turns into an endless competition: at work, in education, even on social media, everyone is rated against everyone else. Someone else’s failure then easily feels like a small breather: “at least I’m not last.” From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that schadenfreude is not only your personal trait but an effect of an environment that sets people against one another. That is no reason to punish yourself, but a reason to notice: you and the one who stumbled are most likely under the same pressure.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: what shared pressure are we both under — me and the person whose failure I was briefly glad about?

contempt.text: Contempt gives a sense of being in the right and of distance, and sometimes it is the only defense when something cuts deep. In his well-known essay “Exiting the Vampire Castle,” Fisher criticized an atmosphere in which people take pleasure in publicly condemning and despising others, displaying their own purity. He believed such contempt divides people who in fact share many of the same difficulties, and changes almost nothing for the better. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that contempt is often aimed at people who are closer to us than they seem. There’s no need to shame yourself for it. But it helps to ask why you and the person you despise ended up on opposite sides. Sometimes a shared weariness shows through the contempt.
contempt.practice: Write down what you might have in common with the person you despise — at least one difficulty or worry.

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong, bodily feeling, and it can be very honest. Fisher spoke ironically of “boring dystopia” — an everyday life in which everything more or less works but provokes a dull revulsion: endless advertising, pointless forms and reports, empty corporate slogans. From his point of view, you could say that disgust is sometimes a healthy reaction to what is genuinely unacceptable, a way of refusing to accept “that’s just how things are.” And if it is turned against yourself, Fisher would remind you: society readily teaches people to despise their own “failures,” even though their causes often lie beyond the person. Your disgust is worth listening to: what does it really concern — you, or the circumstances you have to live in?
disgust.practice: Finish the sentence: “I’m sick of…” — and then ask: is this about me, or about the conditions I’ve ended up in?

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is an understandable reaction to pain and injustice. Fisher noticed that our culture tends to reduce every conflict to personal scores: a particular person is to blame, and payback must be personal. From his point of view, you could say that the thirst for revenge is often aimed at whoever happened to be closest, even though the source of the pain is wider — in conditions that make people hard, worn out and indifferent to one another. This doesn’t excuse the person who hurt you or devalue your feeling. But Fisher invited us to look beyond individuals: personal revenge almost never changes what gives rise to such situations. The energy of this feeling can turn into clarity — about what was unjust and what you need in order to feel safe.
revenge.practice: Write down two things: what specifically was unjust, and what would help you feel safe — without involving the person who hurt you.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to you — a partner, parents, children — and the shame that follows are familiar to a great many people. Fisher spoke of “the privatization of stress”: society declares the pressure of precarious work, debt and constant competition to be everyone’s private business. And that pressure comes home. Home becomes the place where tension built up outside spills over — simply because there’s nowhere else for it to go. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your anger at loved ones is not proof that you love badly, but often the trace of a load you have to carry alone. Understanding this doesn’t excuse harsh words, but it lifts some of the guilt and helps you see: you need support, and the people close to you are not enemies but equally tired people beside you.
anger_at_loved.practice: In the evening, write down: what tension did I bring home from outside today? Where does it really come from?

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is hard, but it doesn’t mean something is wrong with you. Fisher wrote about how the disappearance of collective forms of support shifts the whole weight of life onto individuals. From his point of view, you could say that today the closest relationships often have to stand in for everything at once — support, rest, help and meaning. Under such a load any bond starts to crack. Your ambivalence partly reflects the fact that too much is expected of one person, and that you depend on each other more than you would like. In such a situation love and irritation inevitably intertwine. You can acknowledge both feelings, and consider what load this relationship is carrying for everything that’s missing around it.
ambivalence.practice: List the roles this person fills for you. Are there any among them that someone else could share?

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, after leaving a job, or after a long period of caring for a seriously ill loved one has come to an end often arrives together with sharp guilt. Fisher reminded us how much society shifts onto the shoulders of individuals: caring for the sick, supporting the family, surviving at an exhausting job are all considered private matters that each person must shoulder alone. Under such a load a person becomes depleted, even when they love deeply. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your relief is not evidence of callousness but a natural response to having a burden lifted that was too much for one person. The guilt here is often an echo of the idea that you were obliged to cope endlessly and without help. Love and relief can live side by side. One doesn’t cancel the other.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down how much you carried alone during that period. Read the list as you would read about a close friend.

indifference.text: Sometimes something “should” move you, but inside there is emptiness — and that’s frightening. Fisher described a state many people live in: the stream of news, notifications and entertainment never stops, and feelings seem to grow dull. He wrote about his students, who, as he observed, lived in a mode of constant overload and distraction and could barely concentrate on anything. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your indifference is not necessarily a trait of character but a consequence of an environment that demands you react to everything at once. No psyche can respond endlessly. There’s no need to force yourself to feel “the right way.” You can reduce the stream and give feeling time to return once there’s space.
indifference.practice: Turn off notifications for an hour. At the end of the hour, note: has any feeling appeared that wasn’t there before?

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your role — and leave is familiar to a great many people. Fisher described “capitalist realism” as the feeling that there are no alternatives: however bad things are, they can’t be otherwise. In that light, the dream of escape is not weakness but resistance to that feeling, a way of saying: “there has to be something else.” Fisher valued such utopian impulses and believed that the ability to imagine something different is the first step toward change. From his point of view, you could say there’s no need to break everything immediately. But the wish to escape deserves to be heard seriously: it points to something in the current shape of your life that really is unbearable. You can begin with a question: what exactly do I want to leave behind, and what do I want to find?
escape.practice: Describe in three sentences a day in the life you want to escape to. Note one detail that is there but not here now.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off limits” can be confusing and disorienting. In The Weird and the Eerie, Fisher describes the “weird” as that which doesn’t fit the familiar order — an intrusion of something from outside, after which familiar frames suddenly stop seeming the only ones possible. He stressed that such an experience doesn’t only unsettle but also fascinates. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that attraction to the “wrong” person is often exactly such an encounter with the weird — with something beyond your ordinary life. There’s no need either to condemn it or to rush to do anything about it. You can simply ask yourself: what other possibility, what “outside world,” does this person embody for me?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down: what world, what life, or what part of myself does this attraction open up for me? The answer may be unexpected.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment can make any gathering agonizing. Fisher wrote candidly about the feeling of being out of place: in his essay “Good For Nothing” he described how someone from a family without much money feels like an outsider in spaces where others carry themselves with confidence. He showed that such insecurity is not only a personal trait but the trace of a social hierarchy that from childhood hints at who is “fitting” and who is not. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that part of your fear of judgment is the internalized voice of that hierarchy. Recognizing it is already a relief. And one more thing: a great many people in the room feel the same, it’s just not the done thing to show it. Your shyness doesn’t mean you don’t belong here.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a gathering, ask yourself: whose voice is telling me I don’t belong here? Is it the truth — or an old hierarchy?

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: it’s hard to make plans when you don’t know what will happen. In Capitalist Realism, Fisher cites the sociologist Richard Sennett and his formula “no long term”: modern work and life are increasingly organized around short-term contracts, constant change and the absence of guarantees. Fisher believed this produces chronic anxiety in enormous numbers of people. From this point of view, your uncertainty is not only a personal inability to “plan everything out” but a shared condition of the times. This matters: you are not alone in it and not to blame. Fisher also reminded us that the future is not closed for good: uncertainty also means things may turn out differently from the worst forecasts.
uncertainty.practice: Divide a sheet into two parts: “not up to me” and “up to me today.” In the second, write down at least one thing to do.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — is sometimes harder than even the worst certainty. In Capitalist Realism, Fisher described a Kafkaesque experience everyone knows: calling a call center, endless hold music, being passed from one operator to another — and no one able to decide anything. He saw in this an image of modern bureaucracy, where responsibility is diffuse and all a person can do is wait. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that part of what makes waiting so agonizing is a feeling of powerlessness before an impersonal system, not your impatience. It’s not your fault. You can acknowledge, “Right now nothing depends on me,” — and reclaim at least what does: how you spend this hour.
waiting.practice: Tell yourself: “Right now nothing depends on me.” Then choose one pleasant thing to do in the next hour, and do it.

regret.text: Regret over what you didn’t do often feels like meeting a ghost — the version of your life that could have happened but didn’t. Fisher used the word “hauntology” (from the French hanter, “to haunt”) for the experience of being unable to shake off futures that never came to pass. He wrote about it in relation to culture, but the idea applies to personal life too. Importantly, Fisher didn’t see such ghosts only as a burden: they remind us that something else was possible, and so is possible now. From this point of view, your regret is not simply self-reproach but the trace of a desire that is still alive. You can ask: what did I really want back then — and is there a path for that desire today?
regret.practice: Write down: what did I want at that moment? Then write one small action that is open to that desire today.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person can sound inside you like a distant melody. Fisher wrote a lot about music in which loss can be heard — for example, Burial’s album Untrue, where fragments of voices sound like ghosts of the past. For him such music conveys a particular feeling: the presence of someone who isn’t there. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your longing is not a malfunction to be fixed as soon as possible, but a form of connection with someone who is absent. Fisher valued culture’s capacity to give such feelings a voice rather than drown them out. It may help to find your own “music” of longing — a song, a place, words — where this feeling can sound instead of staying mute inside you.
longing.practice: Find one song that sounds like your longing for this person, and listen to it without doing anything else.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — wars, injustice, grim news — can be enormous and exhausting. Fisher warned about “reflexive impotence”: knowing that everything is bad, combined with the conviction that nothing can be done. Such a conviction, in his view, confirms itself. At the same time, he didn’t suggest taking everything on yourself: Fisher stressed the importance of the collective — thinking things through together, mutual support, shared causes. From this point of view, your pain is a sign that you haven’t grown callous, and that is valuable. But carrying it alone is too much. Relief comes when the pain is shared with others and finds at least a small, manageable expression: a conversation, some help, taking part in something shared.
world_pain.practice: Today, talk about what troubles you in the world with one person you trust. Don’t look for solutions — just share it.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts, and it seems to deliver the final truth about you. Fisher described how, in today’s world, rejection has become an everyday thing: unanswered CVs, interviews, competitions, dating apps. People are constantly being evaluated, and every refusal is easily read as personal inadequacy. Fisher criticized this habit of explaining everything by individual shortcomings while ignoring how the environment is built. From his point of view, you could say that rejection often speaks of how selection works — the number of applicants, chance, other people’s criteria — rather than of your worth. The pain of it is real and deserves attention. But you can put off drawing conclusions about yourself: you are not reducible to a committee’s decision or someone else’s “no.”
rejection.practice: Write down three circumstances that might have influenced this “no” and have nothing to do with your worth.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned can be very strong and very old. Fisher wrote about how modern life leaves people less and less protected: temporary work, frequent moves, the weakening of shared institutions of support. When there is little that’s stable around you, you hold tighter to the few close bonds you have — and fear losing them, because there’s nothing else to lean on. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that your fear is not only personal vulnerability but a response to a general shortage of reliability. This lifts some of the shame about it. And it also suggests a way forward: support can rest not on one person but on a network — friends, a community, shared causes. Fisher believed in the power of the collective, where no one has to hold on alone.
abandonment.practice: Name one person or one community you’ve long wanted to get closer to. Send them a short message.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a feeling that goes on living without an answer. Fisher wrote a lot about pop music and how it gives voice to exactly such experiences: songs of love without return are one of its richest traditions. For him culture is a space where private pain turns out to be shared: listening to a song, you realize someone has already felt exactly this. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that unrequited love is not a personal failure but one of the most common human experiences. Your feeling is real, even if it wasn’t returned. Let yourself lean on those who have expressed something similar — in a song, a book, a film — and feel that you are not alone in this.
unrequited.practice: Find a song or poem about unrequited love that exactly captures your feeling. Reread it or listen to it again.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is the feeling of having been stripped of your dignity, and it can stay in the body for a long time. Fisher wrote about how modern institutions often humiliate people in routine ways: endless audits, reports, evaluations, interviews in which a person must prove again and again their right to a place. He called this bureaucracy of metrics “market Stalinism” — a system in which the numbers matter more than the real work. In such an environment many people feel humiliated even though no one in particular set out to humiliate them. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that humiliation is often built into the system rather than caused by your inadequacy. And if a particular person humiliated you, that speaks of how they use power, not of your worth.
humiliation.practice: Describe the situation in one sentence, starting not with yourself but with the circumstances: “I was put in a position where…”.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body rarely comes out of nowhere. Fisher wrote about how the logic of the market seeps into the most personal areas of life: a person begins to treat themselves as a project that must constantly be improved, promoted and compared with others. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that in such a culture the body too becomes “capital” — something to invest in, judged through other people’s eyes. And constant dissatisfaction with yourself is convenient for the market: it keeps you looking for ever new ways to “fix” yourself. Understanding this doesn’t cancel your feelings, but it removes some of the guilt from them. Your body is not a business project but what you live, feel and connect with others through.
body_shame.practice: Today, notice one ad or image after which you felt worse in your body. Say to yourself: “That’s a sales pitch, not the truth.”

illness.text: When your body lets you down, fear, irritation and fatigue arrive — and often guilt for being “out of action.” Fisher wrote about a culture that demands a person always be in shape, connected and productive. In it, illness is experienced not only as suffering but as personal failure. Speaking of mental health difficulties, Fisher insisted that the blame for them cannot be placed entirely on the individual; this idea can be extended to physical illness as well. From this point of view, you could say that being ill doesn’t mean letting others down. You don’t have to apologize for your body needing time and care. And the help you accept now is not a debt but part of the shared fabric in which people support one another.
illness.practice: If you are offered help, try answering simply “thank you,” without apologies or explanations.

pride.text: Pride in what you’ve done is a good, well-earned feeling. Fisher wrote a great deal about how people, especially from less well-off backgrounds, are taught to think they are “good for nothing,” and how this idea, absorbed in childhood, saps their strength. Against this background, healthy pride in what you’ve done is not vanity but a small act of resistance to an inner verdict. From Fisher’s perspective, you could say that pride also matters because it pushes back against “reflexive impotence” — the conviction that nothing will work out. You did it — so something did work out. Fisher also valued collective joy, so this kind of pride can be shared: tell people who will be glad with you about what you’ve done.
pride.practice: Today, tell one person about something that worked out for you — with no “but” and no playing it down.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a feeling that holds both sorrow and tenderness. Fisher devoted many pages to it: in Ghosts of My Life he writes about music and culture suffused with longing for futures that never came. Following the Italian philosopher Franco “Bifo” Berardi, he spoke of “the slow cancellation of the future” — the sense that the new things once promised never arrived. But Fisher distinguished between a melancholy that resigns itself and one that refuses to forget what was possible. The second keeps the memory that life could have been different — and so still can be. From this point of view, your gentle sadness is a form of faithfulness to what matters. There’s no need to drive it away: a hope lives in it that hasn’t yet found its words.
melancholy.practice: Write down which “never-happened” you are sad about. Then write what in it still seems valuable and possible to you.

quote.text: The slow cancellation of the future
quote.author: Franco “Bifo” Berardi
quote.source: a phrase Fisher develops in Ghosts of My Life
